Unlock these with Subscription Products you've access to Additional Subscription Benefits eBooks Webinars Newsletters Games Monthly Digest Account Settings Go to My Account Bookmarks Manage Subscriptions Need help with your subscription? customersupport@thehindu.co.in 1800 102 1878 The Kerala porotta story: how gourmets cannot get enough of the flatbread’s many versions The Kerala porotta has evolved and now many versions of the classic flatbread is available all over the State Updated - January 05, 2024 03:47 pm IST Saraswathy Nagarajan READ LATER SEE ALL Remove Kerala porotta and curry. | Photo Credit: SREEJITH R KUMAR Flaky, crisp and layered, the Kerala porotta (also called barotta in some places) has a story that is as layered as the porotta itself. Once confined to the Malabar region in North Kerala, today no self-respecting Malayali can claim not to have feasted on this staple that is easily available from Kanhangad in the north to Kaliyikkavila in the south. A hot seller in uppity restaurants and humble thattukadas (makeshift outlets), the porotta has replaced the kanji and the kappa to become the signature dish of the State. In fact, this year, on November 1, observed as Kerala Day, the BBC paid tribute to the State by holding forth on the porotta ’s many charms. Archaeologist and culinary anthropologist Kurush F Dalal says that the porotta is likely to have come with Arab traders from ancient West Asia. He explains: “Kerala has always had trade links with West Asia, right from the pre-Islamic period. So, this must have travelled with the sailors and traders and found a place in North Malabar’s culinary palate.” He points out that though porotta is made of refined flour, Kerala is not a wheat producing state and so its origins clearly lie beyond the seas. Moreover, versions of the porotta can be found all over Malayasia, Singapore and Sri Lanka. Be that as it may. The Malabar porotta now has a special place in the flavour map in Kerala. Over the years, the porotta , made with maida, sugar, milk, oil and more oil, has gone through several makeovers. A porotta maker making porottas at a food stall in Kochi in Kerala. | Photo Credit: MUSTAFAH KK So, there is an entire platter of porottas to feast on: from the crisp nool porotta , resembling strings of hot Mozarella cheese, to the bite-sized coin porotta and the soft bun porotta , the spicy kizhi porotta and the lip-smacking paal porotta soaked in coconut milk and masala. ALSO WATCH Watch| Madurai man teaches you how to flip parottas like a pro Parotta chefs The signature maida porotta is a gourmet’s dream and a nutritionist’s nightmare. Kneaded with oil, salt, milk and sugar, the dough is allowed to rest with a wet cloth over it before it is pulled, punched, stretched and kneaded again to achieve the pliability for flaky, thin flatbreads. Cooks specialising in porotta — their only job is to make porottas — are prized. Quite the showstoppers in some outlets, they showcase with flair the way the dough is teased, kneaded and rolled to achieve the right consistency of the porotta . Yours, Malayalis Anjana George / Updated: May 28, 2017, 11:26 IST Share AA + Text Size Small Medium Large A State where porotta and beef is the ânational dishâ, has been left dumbfounded by the latest directive from the Centre, to ban the sale of cattle for slaughtering A State where porotta and beef is the ânational dishâ, has been left dumbfounded by the latest directive from the Centre, to ban the sale of cattle for slaughtering "Oh! porottayum beefum kazhikkan thonnunu!â There wonât be a single Malayali who wouldnât have uttered or listened to this âclassic Malayali dialogueâ at least once in their life. And the vegetarian minority in the State would only be too familiar with the rants from their beef crazy friends â âAyye, ithuvare beef kazhichittilla? Kashtam!â which would be followed by a drool-worthy description â âtender beef pieces in a thick gravy of ginger, garlic, pepper, and chilly, garnished with thick long fried coconut pieces!â Yes, no matter which part of the world they are in, there is no separating the Malayali from his/her beef. But all of it could very well be a thing of the past; if the much-feared beef ban, a nightmare which has been resisted by Keralites for years becomes a reality, with the implementation of the notification issued by the Union Ministry of Environment, Forests and Climate Change on the regulation of livestock markets. Unsurprisingly, the beef fans of Godâs Own Country are not keeping quiet and have taken to the streets to protest. We bring you some of the funniest reactions of all. âWe might need beef de-addiction centres nowâ âA Malayali without beef is like Metallica without guitars, cricket without Sachin and a Formula One car without wheels,â says the members of the Beef Janata Party, the social media group started earlier in protest against the beef ban. âYou are taking out one of the most important ingredients of the global identity of Malayalis. No wonder, the loudest of outrage against the ban is coming from this part of India,â they say. Meanwhile, several of the die-hard beef lovers are contemplating visiting de-addiction centres, if the beef ban becomes a reality. Pramod G from Trivandrum is one such, who had porotta and beef for breakfast even on his wedding day. âI am a beef addict. I need my beef!â says a disturbed Pramod, who admits that even on festival days like Vishu and Onam, he sneaks away to get a taste of his favourite cuisine. Parvathy S Nayar / TNN / Jul 10, 2013, 00:00 IST Share AA + Text Size Small Medium Large Follow us The anti-porotta campaign is back â this time, with a new allegation that it is high on cancer causing agents! The anti-porotta campaign is back â this time, with a new allegation that it is high on cancer causing agents! For over a year now, the Kerala porotta, which has been a hot favourite among true blue Malayalis, was under the scanner, thanks to campaigns on its ill effects. After a series of attacks, the latest allegation against the Kerala porotta is that it is high on cancer causing agents. Blame it on alloxan Jacob Vadakkanchery, who runs a nature food restaurant in Kochi and has been an advocate of naturopathy himself, ensures that the last item that would find a place in his restaurantâs menu is the Kerala porotta. âMaida is a useless byproduct that is obtained after the extraction of wheat and is devoid of nutrients or bran. Besides, it is rich in a harmful chemical called alloxan, which is rampantly used in laboratory animals like mice to induce diabetics during the testing of anti-diabetic medication. In human beings, alloxan triggers kidney ailments, heart and liver problems and stomach disorders,â he says, adding, âYet, the porotta continues to lure a majority of the Kerala population.â Giving in to temptation True enough, thereâs no denying that the popularity of the porotta cuts across all age groups. Thereâs always this temptation for the forbidden fruit â perhaps why even people who are aware of the so-called health hazards the porotta threatens to cause decide to take an occasional bite into the bread. As Arathy Nair, a student of Mohandas College of Engineering and Technology, Trivandrum, would tell you, âThe porotta is a hot favourite in our college canteen. Besides its yum element, itâs filling enough that hunger pangs wonât trouble you when youâre engrossed in work.â Prod her if she is aware of the so-called ill effects of the porotta and Arathy says, âYes. So Iâm careful enough not to gorge on it every day.â Porotta losing out to appam? Suvarnan Sivaram, F&B Manager of a hotel in Kochi, agrees, saying, âA majority of porotta lovers are usually the young crowd. The older people, who are more concerned about their health than the youngsters, generally avoid it. However, though it features on our menu, of late, itâs not as fast moving an item as the roti or appam.â The porotta began losing its longstanding lure when campaigns throwing light on its ill-effects on oneâs health struck a chord among health conscious Malayalis, who, in turn, gave up on their love for the porottaâ¦ well, at least for a while.
